newsitem.title: USA: US mortgage rates edge higher - Freddie Mac.
newsitem.headline: US mortgage rates edge higher - Freddie Mac.

text.p: U.S. mortgage rates edged higher this week from last week, Freddie Mac said Thursday.
Thirty-year fixed-rate mortgages averaged 7.62 percent in the week ending July 4, up from 7.58 percent last week. Fifteen-year mortgages rates inched up to 7.15 percent from 7.13 percent.
One-year adjustable mortgage rates were barely changed at 5.67 percent, up from 5.66 last week.
A year ago, the 30-year rate averaged 8.14 percent, the 15-year 7.67 percent and the adjustable loan 5.94 percent.

"The economy is currently growing at a moderate pace as evidenced by the Federal Reserve's decision to leave short-term rates at their current level and the employment figures released this morning," Frank Nothaft, Freddie Mac deputy chief economist, said in a statement.

"This alleviates concerns of an overheated market and reduces pressure on interest rates. As a matter of fact, we may even see rates drop back to 7.5 percent in light of the unemployment figures," Nothaft added.

Lenders charged an average 1.8 percent in fees and points on 30-year loans, up slightly from last week. Charges on 15-year loans were unchanged at 1.7 percent. Adjustable loan charges fell to 1.45 percent from 1.5 percent last week.
Freddie Mac is a corporation chartered by Congress that buys mortgages from lenders and packages them into securities for investors.
Separately, the Mortgage Bankers Association of America said the volume of U.S. mortgage applications rose 1.9 percent in the week ended June 27.
The volume of applications to refinance mortgages rose 6.5 percent in the latest survey week, while applications to purchase mortgages inched up 0.5 percent.
